en: The Sūtra of the Supreme King of All Dharmas,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jñānagupta of North India during the Sui Dynasty.
Furthermore, while this Dharma was being taught, the Bhagavat was dwelling in the Bamboo Grove of Kalandaka at Rājagṛha.

At the Ghoṣitārāma, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, headed by the former matted-hair ascetic Uruvilvākāśyapa; they were all arhats whose outflows were exhausted, who had done what was to be done and accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, destroyed the fetters of existence, and through right knowledge their minds were well-liberated. They were all masters of their own minds, having reached the supreme shore—with the sole exception of one person, namely Ānanda the Venerable.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, the Blessed One was about to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and sat in the open air; the community of bhikṣus surrounded him with reverence, all facing toward the Buddha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not long since gone forth; on that very day he had received full ordination. He approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have recently left the household life and received the precepts today; I pray that you will explain to me: how is it that receiving alms-food from a village is called "wholesome food"?
And how is it that by eating such food one becomes a pure field of merit and shall obtain the foremost benefit?
Then that bhikṣu addressed the Buddha with this verse:
“I have not long been ordained, and today I have received full ordination;
O World-Honored One, please explain to me: how may one obtain pure offerings?”
"It is for this purpose that I practice, having left the home life and not maintaining a household;
thus I purify my giving, and I shall further explain its meaning.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said:
“Monks! Listen well and attend with right mindfulness; I shall speak for you.

Just as a monk does not receive the food of a village in vain, and having eaten it, makes a pure offering of it, so too a son or daughter of good family who has gone forth from the home life into homelessness and practices the supreme practice shall attain the ultimate state of excellence. In this way, a monk who enters the Saṅgha, observes the duties of the Saṅgha, and shares in the benefits of the Saṅgha—being endowed with these three qualities—does not receive the food of a village in vain, and having eaten it, makes a pure offering of it, and shall attain the foremost benefit.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“If sentient beings enter the Saṃgha And likewise attend to the activities of the Saṃgha;
Furthermore, they join with the benefits of the Saṃgha, They are able to purify the merit of their giving.”
Then that bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now heard this brief instruction from the Buddha, I do not understand its meaning.”
“World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu enter the Saṃgha, perceive the activities of the Saṃgha, and receive the benefits of the Saṃgha?
Then that bhikṣu spoke this verse:
"How does one enter the Saṅgha and perceive the activity of the Saṅgha?
Tell us the benefits of the Saṅgha, so that having heard them, we may understand. Thus they spoke.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus! Listen well with a focused mind; I shall now explain for you the Saṃgha, the activities of the Saṃgha, and the benefits of the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu said to the Buddha: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"It is thus that one delights in hearing," the Buddha said. "O bhikṣus!"
What is called the Saṃgha?
The Saṃgha consists of the four pairs and eight types of individuals (pudgala); this is what is called the Saṃgha.
"When one gives food with a sincere heart while facing the recipient with palms joined, this is a pure gift;
it is called a field of merit, which all gods and humans must honor.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
“I now speak of the four pairs and the eight classes of individuals;
these are called the Saṃgha, the unsurpassed field of merit. “O Bhikṣus!”
What is called the work of the Saṃgha? That which constitutes the work of the Saṃgha consists of:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.
"This is called the work of the Saṅgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"Always diligently practice the most supreme path, Which is known as the Eightfold Noble Path;"
As that which was said regarding the Saṃgha, their karma is exactly like this.
"Bhikṣus! What is called the benefit of the Saṃgha?"
The benefits for that monk are the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. What are the four?
First, the fruit of the Srotāpanna; second, the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin;
third, the fruit of the Anāgāmin.
"Fourth is the fruit of arhatship;
this is called the great benefit of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One of great body possesses great benefit; such a person of the Saṃgha, like the four fruits of the śramaṇa, is able to purify the merit of giving.
When this had been said, the bhikṣu addressed him, saying:
“Bhagavān, as the Bhagavān has taught:

one who enters the Saṅgha, perceives the activities of the Saṅgha, and unites with the benefits of the Saṅgha, that person properly receives the alms-food offered by the village; having eaten it, he attains the merit of pure giving and reaches the foremost benefit.”
"Bhagavān! If there should be another person who sets out upon the Mahāyāna and leaves the household life in order to attain omniscience, would that *pudgala* be seen within the Saṃgha?"
"Do you see this monk's conduct?
Is it worthy of the Sangha's benefits? Having spoken thus.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, bhikṣu!"
That you are able to call to mind and inquire about this meaning before the Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Samyaksaṃbuddha— O Bhikṣu,
you are most auspicious; your eloquence is supreme and wonderful, for you have skillfully questioned regarding this meaning.
"Monk! Because you have reflected well, you are able to ask the Tathāgata about this meaning. Monk!"
All of this is due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, which has enabled you to give such eloquence in this life as you wish to inquire into the meaning of these phrases;
it is also due to the power of your past vows that you are able to ask in this manner.
"Therefore, bhikṣus!
Listen well and attend carefully; I shall speak for you.
The bhikṣus replied:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
I now wish to hear it.”
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣu! As for what you have thought:..."
"If that person has set their mind upon the Mahāyāna and left the household life to seek omniscience, is that person seen within the Saṃgha?
Is the activity of the Saṃgha seen?"
"Do you see the benefit of the Saṃgha? "No, Bhikṣu!
That person does not see [the Saṃgha] within the Saṃgha; they do not see the activities of the Saṃgha nor the benefits of the Saṃgha at all."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"In that assembly, one does not see [the Sangha], nor does one see the karma of the Sangha;
one does not even see the benefit of the Sangha, because they have set their minds upon Bodhi."
When he had spoken thus, the bhikṣu addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and for what reason do you permit those individuals to go forth and permit them to receive food from villages, yet those individuals are not seen within the Saṃgha?”
"Are the monastic deeds and the benefits of the Saṅgha also not perceived?
World-Honored One!
How is it that such a person (pudgala) can purify the merit of their giving, yet that person is not seen within the Saṅgha?"
"Monastic practice and monastic benefit are likewise not perceived?
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha said: "Bhikṣu!"
"Why do you need to ask this question?
That bhikṣu spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"How can that person purify the merit of their giving?
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Why must you ask this question?"
That bhikṣu spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
That person is not seen within the Saṃgha, nor are the activities of the Saṃgha or the benefits of the Saṃgha seen in him; how, then, can he purify the merit of a gift?"

At that time, having seen that bhikṣu’s threefold request, the World-Honored One immediately manifested a smile and performed a supernatural feat (*ṛddhi*). Having performed such a feat, a great radiance issued from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. That light further possessed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various and extraordinary colors; by its majestic power, it illuminated the entire trichiliocosm, even reaching all sentient beings within the great oceans. None of them had ever before seen or heard of such light, and now, because they saw this light, their hearts were struck with awe and their hair stood on end.

As for those in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, they too, all at a single moment, by the power of the Buddha, knew that this light issued from between the eyebrows of the Buddha; having seen this light, their hearts were struck with awe and their hair stood on end.

At that time, the devas of the Trichiliocosm—from the Cāturmahārājika Heaven up to the Form Realm and the Formless Realm—all proceeded to the Bamboo Grove Kalandaka Monastery in the great city of Rājagṛha. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right countless hundreds of thousands of times, and then stood before the Buddha with right mindfulness, palms joined in reverence. With bodies bowed low, unmoving and unleaning, their eyes never blinking, they gave rise to a mind of respect, a mind of affection, a mind of joy, a mind of exultation, a mind of endurance, a mind of suppleness, a pure mind, and an unobstructed mind. Desiring to hear the Dharma, they withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm, there were gods of great supernatural power, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;

and the lords of the gods, lords of the nāgas, lords of the yakṣas, lords of the gandharvas, lords of the asuras, lords of the kinnaras, lords of the mahoragas, and lords of humans and non-humans—from beneath the earth up to the peak of existence—there was not a single spot as small as a standing staff that was not filled with them.
At that time, all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās within the trichiliocosm,
as well as the various classes of sentient beings dwelling upon the earth throughout the world, beheld the Buddha’s radiance through the Buddha’s supernormal power;
their hearts were struck with awe and their hair stood on end, like a man of great strength [struck by lightning].
In the mere time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, through the Buddha’s majestic power,
they all arrived at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha in a single thought-moment. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
and stood before the Buddha with right mindfulness and palms joined, bowing respectfully and generating a heart of reverence.
With a heart of love, a heart of joy, a heart of elation, a heart of endurance, a heart of pliancy, a pure heart,
and an unobstructed heart, he gazed up at the World-Honored One without blinking his eyes; his body remained motionless as he stood to one side.

At that time, throughout this trichiliocosm, whether within or outside cities, or in the spaces between obstructions, wherever there were large or small rivers and sources of water, they all flowed according to the Dharma with gentle sounds.

Furthermore, within all enclosed spaces and throughout the air, the cries of various birds and other creatures were made harmonious through the Buddha’s supernatural power. Likewise, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and even mountain cattle and water buffaloes remained each in their own place; and the sentient beings in the great oceans likewise, through the Buddha’s power, each stayed in their respective domains without disturbing one another.
At that time, all the devas in this world, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, remained silent, and even the celestial music ceased entirely.

At that moment, all the wicked sentient beings of this world—who possessed fierce and poisonous hearts, delighted in committing various evils, and even perpetrated the five heinous crimes—were all moved by the Buddha’s power in a single thought-moment to love one another as if they were close friends. They gave rise to a mind of benefit, a mind of joy, a gentle mind, a mind capable of virtuous action, a mind of gladness, a pure mind, and an unobstructed mind. With smiling faces and words spoken first, their brows were no longer furrowed; their speech was smooth, neither hurried nor coarse. Whatever they said was pleasing and delightful, so that the young, the old, and those in middle age each found their proper place.

At that time, throughout this great trichiliocosm, there was not even the sound of a cough; by the Buddha’s supernormal power, sentient beings remained in silence. All winds were gentle and fragrant, and sentient beings beheld them with joy, none failing to rejoice. Furthermore, the branches, leaves, medicinal herbs, and so forth of all trees were not stirred by the wind—all such phenomena occurred through the power of the Buddha.
Just as the eighth person who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation has neither inhalation nor exhalation, so too did this great assembly remain in silence;
this was due to the superior power of sustaining the former monk’s past vows and merit, as well as the superior power of sustaining the Buddha’s merit.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, perceiving that everyone was silent, rose from his seat through the Buddha’s spiritual power. Having adjusted his upper robe over one shoulder, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and bowed with single-minded devotion as he gazed up at the Buddha. For the sake of the peace, security, and benefit of the great assembly, and because his mind was pure and unobstructed and he desired to hear the Dharma-gate, he addressed the Buddha regarding the meaning of the questions asked by that bhikṣu, the reason for the Buddha’s emission of light, and the causes and conditions for the gathering of devas and humans, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata does not manifest a smile or emit radiance without cause or condition; what is the cause and condition for this present auspicious sign?
Why do the assembled great multitude remain silent?
Then Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas, the most supreme, do not act without cause; why has this eminent person manifested such auspicious signs?
World-Honored One, please explain this meaning quickly: for what reason have you performed such a great supernatural power?"
Hundreds of thousands of beings, as well as many nayutas,
have now gathered here because they have seen your supernormal powers.
World-Honored One, what is the cause of this?
World-Honored One, for what reason?
For what cause has this great assembly gathered here today?
You, O Buddha, are able to know this meaning; for what reason has the multitude assembled?
The World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, has explained this meaning for my sake.
All the devas and the people of the world have universally given rise to reverence;
with palms joined, they gaze up at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Having completely abandoned their celestial palaces, the sons of gods have come here;
out of reverence and a desire to hear the Dharma, they gaze upon the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
Having departed from the dragon palaces, immeasurable dragons have gathered;
Blessed One, what shall you say regarding the meaning of such a miraculous manifestation?
Having left the yakṣa palace, immeasurable yakṣas have gathered;
Blessed One, what shall you say regarding the meaning of such a miraculous manifestation?
When Śāriputra had spoken these verses, he remained silent.
This Great Being with the Brahma-voice, with a roar like the sound of thundering drums,
explained to Śāriputra the meaning of such miraculous transformations.
“That new bhikṣu has received full ordination today;
Śāriputra questioned me regarding him as one who is a bodhisattva.”
"How does one go forth?
What is the nature of that karma;
and how does one receive alms-food from a village?"
"How is pure giving attained?
For this reason, Śāriputra, he emitted a ray of light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows;
this light of great power and majesty shone throughout the world-systems.
For this purpose, Śāriputra, the hosts of devas have all assembled;
with palms joined in the ten fingers, they gaze up at the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings.
For this purpose, Śāriputra, the nāgas and yakṣas have come together.
Desiring to roar with the sound of clouds and thunder, Śāriputra went to where the Tathāgata was.
For this reason, an inconceivable number of billions of beings gathered;
they all attained arhatship, their outflows exhausted, having reached nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra, for this reason, an inconceivable number of billions have gathered;
all should give rise to this intention as a cause and condition for pratyekabuddhahood.
Śāriputra, for this reason, an inconceivable number of billions have gathered.
One should armor oneself with self-restraint for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Śāriputra, because of this meaning, an inconceivable multitude has gathered;
they shall not regress from the Mahāyāna and shall attain supreme enlightenment.
Having heard the meaning of these words, for this reason the Buddha gave his prediction:
that those of firm resolve who repent of their evil deeds, as many as hundreds of millions, shall attain such [a state].
Having heard the meaning of these words, in the future age of the final dharma;
Among billions of sentient beings dwelling on the most supreme path,
excluding those bodhisattvas, it will be impossible for anyone else in the future final age to be able to uphold this sutra.
Except for those bodhisattvas, in the future age of the final dharma,
those who hear this sutra will lack wisdom and have no faith.
Those beings possess little faith and are unable to resolve upon bodhi.
If, upon hearing this sutra, one repeatedly gives rise to doubt and hesitation;
if one does not believe in this sutra, one will dwell eternally in birth and death,
with the hells as one's dwelling place and the animal realm as one's garden.
In the realms of gods and humans, they have all shattered [all attachments] without exception.
Those who do not reject this sutra will, in the future age of the final dharma,
all those gods and humans alike, attain arhatship.
If one were to speak before them, they too would give rise to doubt;
even if there were Pratyekabuddhas filling the worlds of the ten directions,
if one were to speak before them, their minds would likewise give rise to doubt.
There is no one who, without having cultivated goodness, can hear such a teaching;
only those who are steadfast and have accomplished the goal are able to listen to this path.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas, I have preached this Dharma-sūtra.
"Having practiced therein, he shall become a Honored One among Two-legged Beings.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"That newly ordained bhikṣu, who has not long since left the household life and received the precepts today, came to question me:"
“Śāriputra, how is it that those who have set out in the Mahāyāna receive alms-food from villages and yet call it ‘wholesome food,’ and having eaten it,
are able to purify the merit of their giving? Śāriputra!
Because that bhikṣu asked about this matter, immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings have gathered here, all desiring to hear me explain this meaning.
Śāriputra! If I were now to explain, reveal, and analyze this meaning so that it may be easily understood by those of shallow capacity, that immeasurable multitude would obtain great benefit.
When he had spoken thus, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now is the very time; we pray that you will explain it for us.”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! If I were to explain the meaning of these words now, there might be some sentient beings whose minds would become confused and distressed."
Why is this? This great donor is inconceivable; his generosity, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, wisdom, and his great lion’s roar are all inconceivable.

This great assembly of sentient beings possesses inconceivable dharmas; ordinary worldlings and those of the two vehicles are unable to discern, believe in, enter into, or understand them, with the sole exception of non-retrogressive Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and others.
"Śāriputra! Because I see this, although he has requested three times, I remain silent and do not speak.
Śāriputra spoke again:
"Bhagavān, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we pray that you will explain this for us, even unto the point that many sentient beings may attain right faith."
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra! If I were to explain the meaning of these phrases, sentient beings would become bewildered and distressed."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas such as giving are inconceivable; even because I have seen this, he remained silent and did not speak despite being requested three times. Śāriputra spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
For the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many sentient beings, out of compassion for them, we pray that you will explain this.

In future ages, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have set out in the Mahāyāna; upon hearing the meaning of these phrases, they will give rise to a heart of affection and respect, shall attain right faith, cultivate various deeds, and adorn themselves with the great armor.”
At that time, having seen Śāriputra’s request three times, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva need not purify their giving.”
Why is this? Because from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the Way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s giving is ultimately and eternally pure. Why is this?

Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings, even if all sentient beings were to offer them every kind of article of comfort as an act of worship, they still could not repay the Bodhisattvas' kindness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"If there are those who resolve their minds, It becomes the causal condition for the Buddha's wisdom;
From the moment they first resolve their minds, They purify their giving."
If there are those who resolve their minds, they possess the causal conditions for the Buddha-way;
they need not perform further acts of pure giving, for from the beginning, pure giving has already been perfected.
All devas and worldly people must always maintain a mind of diligent effort.
Serving that heroic one, the Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom—
through him, all those in the realms of gods and humans are perfected;
when the wise person gives rise to the mind of enlightenment even once, they are already able to purify all acts of giving.
"Without relying on the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm;
through a mind free from dependence, all such gifts are purified.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Śāriputra! I shall provide you with a simile to fulfill this meaning. Why is that?
I provide this analogy so that those who possess wisdom may correctly understand its meaning.

"Śāriputra, suppose a bodhisattva were to receive robes offered by sentient beings as large as the continent of Jambudvīpa, using them daily from the first moment of generating the mind of awakening; such robes as these can all be given as pure gifts."
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. “Śāriputra!

Even if a bodhisattva were to receive from sentient beings offerings of food as vast as Mount Sumeru, and were to consume them day after day from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, such food and drink could all be considered pure gifts.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. "Śāriputra!..."

Suppose a bodhisattva accepts a seat offered by sentient beings that is as wide as the four continents and as high as Mount Sumeru, adorned with the seven treasures like that mountain itself, and spread with celestial garments so fine and soft; if from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment they daily utilize such a wondrous seat, they are able to purify that gift.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. "Śāriputra!..."

If there were such multi-storied jeweled palaces, as well as immeasurable towers, windows, and balconies, adorned with various colors by banners, canopies, bells, and nets; surrounded by sevenfold walls of the seven precious gems, like the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and further possessing immeasurable *kalpavṛkṣa* trees, musical trees, trees of incense, flowers, and fruits, and garland trees, with immeasurable incense vases placed everywhere; filled with lotus ponds containing water of eight qualities—exquisite, cool, clear, stainless, and free of mud—with various flowers covering the surface and golden sand spread upon the bottom, the water so transparent and pure it is like lapis lazuli; with railings of the seven precious gems encircling them in seven tiers, perfectly aligned on all four sides with four stairways, and within every lotus pond there is a jeweled palace.

Furthermore, there were seven rows of jewel ponds surrounding it, hung with various silken banners and adorned with precious vases; they were decorated with diverse colors and were most delightful to behold. Within them were couches and seats made of the seven treasures, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of nayutas, arranged according to the directions—east, west, south, and north—and perfumed with burning incense, strewn with flowers, and covered with jeweled canopies.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were such jeweled palaces and jeweled couches, and sentient beings were to offer them all to a bodhisattva; the bodhisattva would accept them and, from the first moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, use them day after day, being able to purify every gift.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva is the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings. "Śāriputra!
You should now know that all mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas arise from the Bodhisattva.

That is to say: great families of Kṣatriyas, great families of Brāhmaṇas, and great families of householders; whether kings, or wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin); or the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; as well as the gods of the Form Realm and the Formless Realm; or those who abide in the first fruit up to the fourth fruit [of the śrāvaka path].
If they are to become pratyekabuddhas or attain the state of a pratyekabuddha;
or if they are to attain the knowledge of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma.

If people hear the true Dharma preached by them and are able to practice according to what they have heard, having practiced, they will immediately abide in the four fruits of a śrāvaka, or even give rise to the aspiration for the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Some may give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

If they hear the teaching on generosity, they immediately practice the deeds of giving; having practiced them, they are born into the families of kṣatriyas, brahmins, or householders, and even attain the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin).

If they hear the teaching on ethical discipline, they immediately practice the deeds of morality; having practiced them, they are born in the heavens of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (paranirmita-vaśavartin).
If they hear the exposition of the four immeasurables and are able to practice according to what they have heard, having practiced, they will be reborn in the realm of form or the formless realm.
Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that all these are born from the Bodhisattva.
“Śāriputra! For example, it is like the Nāga King Anavatapta, who by his majestic power brings forth the four great rivers. What are these four?
That is to say:
the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Vakṣu, and Sītā; each of these four rivers has five hundred small rivers as its retinue.
The great river Gaṅgā and its tributaries flow into the eastern ocean, filling it;
the great river Sindhu and its tributaries flow into the southern ocean, filling it;
and the great river Vakṣu and its tributaries flow into the western ocean, filling it.
The four great rivers and their tributaries flow into the Northern Sea, filling that ocean.
What do you think?
As these four great rivers and their tributaries enter the sea in succession, does this bring benefit to the sentient beings of the four quarters in the places they pass through?
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One! You bring boundless benefit to all sentient beings;
whether human or non-human, all receive great nourishment. All the various crops by the rivers—rice, hemp, beans, wheat, and other field plants—all receive this moisture.”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"
"Who could fill those four great oceans? Śāriputra said,
"World-Honored One!"
"These four great rivers cause that ocean to be filled.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
Are those four great oceans of benefit to sentient beings? Śāriputra replied:
"It shall bring great benefit to all sentient beings dwelling in water and on land.
These include:
turtles, fish, and their like, as well as fishermen; furthermore, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, piśācas, nāgas, snakes, mahoragas, and other immeasurable varieties of sentient beings."
If there are sentient beings whose palaces and dwellings are filled with various treasures—

namely, coral, vaidūrya, indranīla, musāragalva, maṇi-jewels, shells, and other such rarities— as well as countless other precious abodes, all of which emerge from the great ocean to provide benefit for various classes of beings, so that people receive immense benefit from their use.
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"
“From where do the four great rivers flow forth? Śāriputra said,
“World-Honored One!”
"It emerges from Lake Anavatapta.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
The Nāga King Anavatapta is freed from three fears.
What are these three? They are as follows:
The fear of the garuḍa, the fear of being burned by hot sand, and the fear of taking the form of a snake during sexual intercourse—
Śāriputra, they have all been freed from these three fears. Śāriputra!
The palace of the Nāga King Anavatapta is inhabited solely by those possessing supernormal powers and meditative concentration; whoever enters it or beholds it shall not be burned.
Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One!
That great nāga palace is endowed with rare, extraordinary, and supreme dharmas."

As for what is called the fear of the various nāgas, none of these things exist for that Great Nāga King; neither do the sentient beings born there, nor those who enter it, experience such fear, because it is a dwelling place for those possessed of supernatural powers and majestic virtue.
"World-Honored One!

The Great Dragon King Anavatapta possesses immeasurable merit and is fully endowed with it; he sends forth the four great rivers toward the oceans of the four directions, benefiting sentient beings and enabling them to attain peace and happiness."
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is, Śāriputra!"
One should know that it is the same for the bodhisattva mahāsattva. Śāriputra!
Just as the great nāga king Anavatapta is freed from the three fears, so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva freed from the three fears.
What are these three? They are:
the fear of hell, the fear of the animal realm, and the fear of the world of Yama.

Śāriputra! Just as the great lake Anavatapta produces four great rivers that flow forth in the four directions, so too does a bodhisattva gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction.
What are the four? They are:
giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.
Śāriputra! Just as that great ocean originates from the great lake Anavatapta, so too does the universal knowledge of all Buddhas arise from the bodhisattva.

Śāriputra! Just as that great ocean, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis, is the place where all sentient beings dwell and possess complete peace and happiness, you should know that likewise all classes of beings born within the three realms of existence dwell in reliance upon the universal wisdom of the Buddhas—namely:
the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that all the articles of comfort and well-being within the trichiliocosm are produced entirely through the Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva generates the aspiration for enlightenment, they immediately engage in practice;
having engaged in practice, they then receive a prediction of enlightenment.
Having received the prediction, they immediately attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
having attained *bodhi*, they then turn the wheel of Dharma.
Such a wheel of Dharma has never before been turned; neither by śramaṇas, nor by brāhmaṇas, nor by devas, nor by Māras, nor by Brahmās, nor by any other beings, is it possible for them to turn it.

When he turns the wheel of Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, the teaching he proclaims is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; it is complete in meaning and phrasing, singularly pure, and explains the holy life so that the fourfold assembly may understand it.
What are these four? They are the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

By means of these causes and conditions, immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings will experience the bliss of devas and humans without interruption, forever severing all suffering and never being parted from various joys.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
From where does such delight in the Dharma arise?
Śāriputra said: “World-Honored One,
they are born from the bodhisattva.”
“Śāriputra! What do you think?
From whom do you see those dharmas that emerge from the three realms of existence arise?”
Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One,
they are born from the Bodhisattva."
“Śāriputra! What do you think?

If one were to offer all the requisites for worship produced within the three realms of existence to a bodhisattva as an offering, would that be able to repay the bodhisattva for the benefits and kindness previously bestowed?”
Śāriputra said: “No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Because it arises from that,
World-Honored One!

Suppose there is a poor person who lacks all wealth and possessions, and a wealthy man, moved by great compassion, bestows upon that poor person hundreds of thousands of immeasurable and innumerable treasures. Furthermore, he does the same for a second and a third poor person, continuing until he has given various treasures to hundreds of thousands of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, making them all prosperous and sufficient. He causes them to be entirely freed from the sufferings of fear, strife, and bondage;
he further frees them from all the manifold sufferings of the evil realms and enables them to possess the immeasurable joys of devas and humans.

Suppose among those sentient beings there were a single person who took a crystal bead and broke it into a hundred pieces; taking one part from among those hundred pieces, they brought it to the person who had previously bestowed kindness upon them and said to that person:
"In the past, you performed a beneficial service for me; I have now come specifically to repay you for this."
"World-Honored One!
That person has brought great benefit to sentient beings; if another were to give even a single portion of crystal to that man, would this constitute a repayment?"
The Buddha said, "No. Śāriputra said:
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is."
Sugata! You should know that as for those bodhisattvas who bring great benefit to all sentient beings, even a single person could not repay their kindness with even a portion of crystal water.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

If those who have set out in the Great Vehicle are constantly pursued and provided with all manner of desired requisites— even unto the end of their lives— by sentient beings, even though such things are done, they cannot repay that kindness."
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
They follow the Buddha’s teaching well, performing deeds as those who are disciples of the Buddha do. Śāriputra!

If all sentient beings were to offer their own skin, flesh, sinews, blood, and marrow, or even sacrifice their bodies up to a hundred thousand times, desiring to repay the benefits conferred by a bodhisattva, they would not repay even one part in a hundred; nor could they repay it even in a part of a hundred thousand koṭis, an asaṃkhyeya part, or by means of calculation or analogy.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Those who resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! For example, suppose there were a sandalwood tree in this Jambudvīpa; when its sprouts emerge, whatever ailments boys or girls may have are all cured by these tree sprouts.
When its leaves emerge, whatever ailments men, women, boys, or girls may have are all cured by these tree leaves.
When the tree has grown large, those who enter its shade find all the afflictions of sentient beings healed and cured;

later, when it bears fruit, its light shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and any sentient being who contemplates this light shall likewise attain freedom from old age, sickness, and death;
if one cuts down this tree to take its wood, one will not fear poverty, and even after the wood has been split, it still possesses these benefits.

If one were to take that wood and build a house with it, anyone who enters its interior will have all fears completely eliminated, and they shall likewise experience neither cold nor heat, nor hunger nor thirst.
In this same way, Śāriputra!

When the sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits of that candana tree grow large, whether they are cut down or piled up to form a dwelling, there is nothing that does not bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
Thus, Śāriputra, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they gather in sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu).
What are these four? They are:
giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation, which cause all those sentient beings to attain peace and happiness.
Having caused them to rejoice, they are then able to enter the three gates of liberation in accordance with the Dharma.
What are these three? They are as follows:
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
As these increase, one attains the perfection of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and ultimately achieves the fruit of omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Having attained the fruit, one shall enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of great nirvana without remainder.
At the time of passing away, one shall cause one's own śarīra relics to be broken into pieces the size of mustard seeds, which shall likewise serve as a support for the Dharma.
Śāriputra! It is like the candana tree:
once its wood has been cut and carried away to various directions, and one enters a house made of that wood, the feverish afflictions of desire will no longer arise.
The relics of the Tathāgata are also like this,
Śāriputra! For this reason,
you should know that if sons or daughters of good family give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they thereby repay the kindness previously bestowed upon them.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

One who resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not sever the practice of the Tathāgata’s teachings, nor does he sever the stages of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*; rather, he is able to sever all the sufferings of sentient beings, as well as the sufferings of humans and devas.
Śāriputra! What do you think?
Is there anyone else who resembles that person?
Śāriputra said: "No, World-Honored One."

Whether they be humans, devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or any other beings, even if they were to provide that bodhisattva with all manner of articles of pleasure, none could ever repay the kindness of the benefit he previously bestowed upon them.

“Śāriputra! If, for one eon or less than an eon, or for a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, or even for a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta eons, one were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure, would one be able to obtain a reward?”
Śāriputra said: "No, World-Honored One."
The Buddha said: "Therefore, Śāriputra!

If sons of good family or daughters of good family wish to repay the kindness they have received from them, they should resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; in this way, they may repay that prior kindness in a manner equal to theirs."
Śāriputra said: “So it is, World-Honored One!”
You should know that as one has been given by another, one must repay them with something similar to what was given.
If one wishes to repay the kindness of those who are peerless in the world, one must instead give rise to a mind that is unsurpassed and peerless;

if one wishes to offer the unsurpassed repayment to the Buddhas of the future, those sons and daughters of good family must likewise give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Only in this way can it be called repaying their kindness.
“Śāriputra! There are two kinds of persons who offer the unsurpassed offering to the Tathāgata.
What are these two?
"There are persons who have reached the exhaustion of all outflows, and there are persons who give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"There are two kinds of persons Who are able to make offerings to the Buddha."
The exhaustion of outflows and the arousal of the bodhicitta— these are called the two kinds [of gifts].
Within all the worlds of the three realms of existence,
there is no material gift by which one can repay the kindness of that Great Being.
To give various forms, scents, tastes, and so forth— those things which are beloved and pleasing to the mind—
to such a person is not yet called making an offering. However,
if one generates the bodhicitta for the sake of the fruit of enlightenment;
This is to have no seeking at all, which is called the supreme offering.
Even if one were to give everything required by the devas, the people of the world,
and the realms of the Māras, it would still not be called repaying their kindness.
He lacks nothing, nor does he give rise to desire;
therefore, toward such a Great Being, it is not called making an offering.
If there is someone who wishes to obtain the merit of making an offering to the Buddha, [they should act as follows].
One who desires that [merit] must seek awakening;
if one wishes to perform deeds of merit repeatedly and immeasurably,
one must resolve for awakening and swiftly cultivate reverence.
If one wishes to seek the various dhyānas, And desires to cultivate immeasurable mindfulness;
One must give rise to diligence, As the causal condition for the Buddha’s wisdom.
If one wishes to obtain all forms of bliss And destroy all forms of suffering;
One should give rise to this aspiration for the sake of the Buddha’s bodhi.
If one wishes to see immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya Buddhas,
one should cultivate a mind of reverence and joyfully resolve upon bodhi.
If a person wishes to travel to those boundless worlds,
they must arouse great diligence and take joy in generating the bodhicitta.
If a person’s heart finds joy in the bodhi of the Buddhas of the past;
One must resolve to attain bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
If anyone wishes to swiftly behold the Buddhas of the future,
they must resolve to attain bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
If a person wishes to behold the Buddhas of the present,
they must always maintain joy and cultivate bodhi.
If a person gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness, wishing to encompass all sentient beings;
One must give rise to this desire for the sake of the Buddha’s bodhi.
If one wishes to cause sentient beings to be liberated from all sufferings,
one must repeatedly study that unsurpassed wisdom.
If one wishes to bestow upon sentient beings Immeasurable and boundless happiness,
One must give rise to this aspiration And seek the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.
If a person wishes to abandon All the various evil realms of existence,
One must give rise to this aspiration, seeking after bodhi.
Those merits are boundless; they cannot be fully recounted.
If one gives rise to such an intention, one shall awaken to supreme bodhi.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, Śāriputra addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when this Dharma-gate was taught, how many sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra! Why do you now need to ask about such a matter?"
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If the Tathāgata, with his great wisdom, were to speak of this, the minds of boundless sentient beings would all become deluded.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
All the morality, concentration, wisdom, and supernormal powers possessed by the Tathāgata are entirely immeasurable.
Śāriputra! What do you think?
Is there anyone who can know the limit of space?
Śāriputra said: "No, World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Within the past, there has been no one who knows the limits of space; likewise, in the future and the present, no one knows them.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Śāriputra!
Of the great wisdom of the Tathāgata, there are no sentient beings— whether śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas— among those of the past, future, or present who possess knowledge of it."
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This is the wisdom of the Buddha;
it is not within the sphere of the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is unprecedented.”
"Those sentient beings who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* shall attain such wisdom of excellent discernment.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"
"It is so, it is so! Just as you have said, those sentient beings shall attain such well-determined wisdom, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
How should those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the wisdom of thorough discernment?
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
Suppose all sentient beings in this Jambudvīpa— whether on land, in water, in the air, or on the earth— were to gradually practice and all attain human form.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there were someone who taught another to uphold the five precepts or to abide in the ten wholesome paths of action,
would that son or daughter of good family accrue much merit by reason of this causal condition?
Śāriputra said: "Very many, Blessed One!"
"Very much so,
Sugata! It is even beyond the reach of analogy."
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra! I shall now speak further so that you may delight in hearing it."

If all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were taught the five precepts and established in the ten paths of wholesome action, the merit obtained by such a person would be surpassed by that of another person—a son of good family or daughter of good family—who teaches even a single person to abide on the stage of practice through faith; the merit of the latter is greater than that of the former.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
If one were to establish all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa in the stage of practice through faith, would their merit be great?
Śāriputra said: “Very many, Blessed One!”
"Very much so, Sugata!
The merit of that person cannot be illustrated by analogy; it is immeasurable, boundless, and far greater than the former."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught but a single person to abide on the stage of Dharma-practice, their merit would be greater than that."
If one teaches all sentient beings to dwell on the stage of practice in accordance with the Dharma, the merit is greater than that;
if one teaches all sentient beings to dwell on the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*), the merit is greater than that;

if one teaches all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to dwell in the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), the merit is greater than that; and if one teaches a single person to dwell in the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the merit is greater than that.

If one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the second fruit, and another were to establish a single person in the third fruit, the latter’s merit would be greater than the former’s.

If one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the third fruit, and another were to establish a single person in the fourth fruit, the latter’s merit would be greater than the former’s.

If one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the fourth fruit, and another were to establish a single person in the path of a pratyekabuddha, the latter’s merit would be greater than the former’s.

If one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the path of the pratyekabuddhas, yet if one were to establish a single person in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the merit of the latter would be greater than that of the former;

if one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet if one were to establish a single person in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), the merit of the latter would be greater than that of the former;

if one were to establish all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa in the stage of non-retrogression, yet if one were to cause a single person to swiftly attain omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), the merit of the latter would be greater than that of the former.

To teach all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa so that they may swiftly attain omniscience, and for any person who, regarding this Dharma-gate, gives rise to bodhisattva wisdom, destroys the karma of Māra, abandons the five aggregates and the non-shared realms, leaves behind the sense bases, destroys the afflictions, gathers and assists the white dharmas while extinguishing those that assist the black dharmas, and extensively expounds this *Sarvadharma-paramarāja-sūtra* to others—the merit obtained thereby is infinitely greater than the former.

“Śāriputra! Setting aside Jambudvīpa and even the four continents, consider likewise a thousandfold world system, a two-thousandfold world system, or a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, and even the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River in the eastern direction—whether they possess form or are formless, whether they have perception, lack perception, or are neither percipient nor non-percipient; whether they dwell in water or on land; whether they are born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation.”
Those of such a kind who practice gradually all attain human bodies; likewise, sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who practice gradually also all attain human bodies.
Śāriputra, if someone were to teach others to abide in the five precepts and be complete in the ten paths of wholesome action,
what do you think?
Would the merit obtained by that person be great?
Śāriputra said: "Very many, Blessed One!"
"Very many, Sugata! They are immeasurable,
boundless, and beyond all analogy."
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, upon hearing this *Sarvadharmāgra-rāja-sūtra*, do not slander it, but rather listen to it further, receive it, uphold it, read it, recite it, or explain it to others—for their prior merit, [the merit of those who merely hear] does not equal even one hundredth part; nor one thousandth, nor one hundred-thousandth, nor one koṭi-th, nor one hundred-thousand-nayuta-koṭi-th part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose one were to instruct all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to abide in the stage of practice through faith, the stage of the eight persons, the four fruits, and the stage of the pratyekabuddhas; and even further, causing them to resolve their minds toward the Dharma of non-retrogression, the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the swift attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

If there are sons or daughters of good family who receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this *Sarvadharmāgrarāja Sūtra* to others, this mass of merit shall be more excellent, more supreme, more abundant, more sublime, most exquisite, incomparable, unsurpassed, the highest of the unsurpassed, and peerless compared to the former mass of merit; among the peerless, they shall obtain peerless merit.

Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that those sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and give rise to faith possess this wholesome, decisive wisdom and have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Śāriputra! Such sentient beings should be called non-retrogressive; they should be called liberated; they should be called crossed over; they should be called tranquil;
they should be called profoundly tranquil; they should be called bathed; they should be called tamed; they should be called...”
One should say he is unsurpassed; one should say he is the most unsurpassed; one should say he has reached nirvāṇa; one should say he has already attained parinirvāṇa;
one should say he is able to preach the Dharma; one should say he is able to explain the meaning; one should say he speaks what is real; one should say he speaks what is true;
one should say he acts according to his word; one should say he has laid down the heavy burden; one should say he is free from desire.

It should be called "free from hatred," it should be called "free from delusion," it should be called "stainless," it should be called "washed and purified," it should be called "having reached the other shore," it should be called "the hearer," it should be called "one who has vomited out desire," it should be called "one who has vomited out hatred," it should be called "one who has vomited out delusion," it should be called "one who has washed away all evils," and it should be called "a son of the Buddha."
One should say: "Field of Merit"; one should say: "Fierce and Valiant"; one should say: "Heroic Man"; one should say:
"Possessor of Superior Form"; one should say: "Conqueror of Enemy Armies"; one should say: "Lion"; one should say: "Man";
one should say: "Great Man"; one should say: "Victorious Man"; one should say: "Fearless Man. One should say: [and so forth].
A man of resolve should be called a man of great resolve; he should be called a well-tamed man; he should be called a bull-king among men;
he should be called a transcendent man; he should be called a heroic man capable of subduing others;
he should be called a lion among men; he should be called a bull among men; he should be called a dragon; and he should be called a deva.

...should be called the "God among Gods," should be called a "Brahmin," should be called "One Who Has Departed from Evil," should be called "Unobstructed," should be called "Unbound," should be called "Free from Avarice," should be called "Free from Poison," should be called "Not Deluded," should be called "Incomparable," should be called "Never Separated," and should be called "One Who Does Not Speak Mixed Words. ...
One should say "words of right mindfulness"; one should say "unsurpassed words"; one should say "supremely unsurpassed words";
one should say "most excellent words"; one should say "unstained words"; one should say "unattached words"; one should say "unbound words";
one should say "words of definitive realization"; one should say "all that is spoken is true"; one should say "all that is spoken is..."
Truly, it should be said that he is endowed with all merits; it should be said that he has performed what was to be done; it should be said that his task is accomplished;
it should be said that he has mastered all that must be done; it should be said that he is possessed of shame and dread of blame;
it should be said that he acts much; it should be said that he performs much benefit; it should be said that he is compassionate; it should be said that he is endowed with all dharmas of merit.
...one should say "having abandoned all that is non-meritorious"; one should say "endowed with all things";
one should say "unstained"; one should say "universally unstained"; one should say "not timid"; one should say "not fearful"; one should say "not startled";
one should say "not terrified"; one should say "not weak"; one should say "not distracted"; one should say...
Endowed with immeasurable and boundless meritorious dharmas and practices, he should be called Mount Cloud,
Mount Sumeru, Mount Meru, Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Mahācakravāḍa,
the Immovable One, the Giver, the Master of Giving, and the One Possessing All.

Regarding renunciation, it should be called "giving well," "having a serene and joyful countenance," "being endowed with giving," "observing the precepts," "patience," "diligence," "concentration," "wisdom," "cultivating supernormal powers," "having attained mastery of supernormal powers," and "reaching all places."

One should say "Great Power Attained," one should say "Power Reached," one should say "Arrived at the Place of Peace," one should say "Already Crossed to the Other Shore," one should say "Training in the Manner of All Buddhas," one should say "Never Ceasing the Practice of the Buddhas," one should say "Having Fully Attained the Fulfillment of Vows in All Buddha-Dharmas," one should say "Shattered the Enemy Māra," and one should say "Crushed All..."
Regarding "poisonous thorns," it should be said: "causing the power of Māra to weaken"; it should be said: "dispersing the hosts of Māra’s army";
it should be said: "causing Māra to perish"; it should be said: "sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)"; it should be said: "having already repelled the poisonous thorns";
it should be said: "eliminating the enemy Māra"; it should be said: "conforming to awakening"; it should be said: "causing those who follow the stream to turn back."
It should be called "逆流" (Going Against the Stream); it should be called "岸" (The Shore); it should be called "能度" (Able to Cross Over);

it should be called "已度" (Already Crossed Over); it should be called "自得脫教" (Self-Attained Teaching of Liberation); it should be called "破暗" (Destroying Darkness); it should be called "月" (Moon); it should be called "日" (Sun);
it should be called "無邊光" (Boundless Light); it should be called "無礙光" (Unobstructed Light); it should be called "不可思光" (Inconceivable Light); and it should be called "難稱" (Difficult to Praise).
Light should be called immeasurable light; it should be called light that reaches all places; it should be called universal light;
